prompt: Which of the following is NOT one of the “top six” things employees value, according to guest speaker Sam Lewis?
explanation: Lewis’s top six are Challenge, Location, Advancement, Money, People and Security. Stock options are not on the list.

prompt: Guest speaker Sam Lewis described hiring a woman for less money because she hated her boss. According to Lewis, which employee value outweighed money in her decision?
explanation: People means who you work with and for. Her dislike of her boss mattered more to her than the pay difference.

prompt: Sam Lewis called ______ the “sneaky” value that sits at the top of many employees’ lists without them realizing it.
explanation: Security is the sneaky one: some people won’t move for any amount of money.

prompt: An early-career employee looks at a flat organizational chart and concludes, “I’m not going anywhere.” According to Sam Lewis, which employee value matters most at this stage of a career?
explanation: Advancement matters most early in a career, and priorities shift as a career goes on.

prompt: An organization gives employees a raise for each additional year on the job. Under Sam Lewis’s three compensation models, which model is it following?
explanation: Lewis’s three models are Time & Tenure, Performance and Competency; yearly raises are Time & Tenure. Gainsharing is a group incentive, not one of his three models, and most good systems combine all three.

prompt: Sam Lewis’s “manager’s test” for seniority pay asks which question?
options: Can the employee’s certified skill actually be used on the job?
Is the starting year used as the baseline for targets reasonable?
No test is needed, because federal law requires an automatic raise after every year of service
What does an additional year of experience change in this role?
explanation: If an extra year changes nothing in the role, pay stays put: the job is the limiter, not the person. The skill-use and baseline questions belong to Lewis’s competency and performance-pay tests.

prompt: After a plant installs new equipment, output jumps and production workers ask for the productivity bonus. According to Sam Lewis’s tests for performance pay, which test does this bonus fail?
explanation: The four performance-pay tests are Influence, Clarity, Balance and Baseline; the workers didn’t cause the gain, so Influence fails (the new equipment also shifts the baseline). Relevant and Used are competency-pay tests.

prompt: A production line runs at 110% of rate but produces 80% scrap because its bonus rewards only speed. Which of Sam Lewis’s performance-pay tests does the plan fail?
explanation: Balance means the measure can’t reward one result (speed) at the expense of another (quality).

prompt: A compensation manager sets a bonus target using the 2008 housing crash as the starting year. According to Sam Lewis, which test does this plan fail?
explanation: A bad starting year makes the targets far too easy, so the plan fails the Baseline test.

prompt: Sam Lewis held 8 meetings a month, including one at 11 p.m., to explain to employees how their bonus was calculated. Which performance-pay test was he addressing?
explanation: Clarity: people must understand how the payout is calculated.

prompt: Sam Lewis’s plant-wide STAR bonus (productivity + quality + expenses, with everyone in the pool) was modeled on the ______.
explanation: STAR was a Scanlon-style gainsharing plan. Lewis also cited Herzberg and open-book management, and he prefers bonuses for smaller groups.

prompt: An employer gave extruder operators a raise for certifying on the calender line, but none of them was ever moved there. According to Sam Lewis, which competency-pay test does this fail?
explanation: The three competency tests are Relevant, Applied and Used. The company never used the skill, so Lewis eliminated the pay.

prompt: All maintenance workers were paid for completing hydraulics training, but a later evaluation showed almost none of them could actually do the work. Which of Sam Lewis’s competency-pay tests does this fail?
explanation: The skill was never truly Applied. Lewis’s lesson: evaluate first, then pay.

prompt: According to Sam Lewis, pay rises as a job shifts from managing ______.
options: None of the answer choices are correct
explanation: Entry-level jobs manage things, managers manage people and the CEO manages mostly ideas. This ties to point systems like Hay.

prompt: A company introduces an individual bonus for each completed work order. What is the most likely unintended consequence?
options: Cherry-picking of easy orders and rushed repairs
A move to Broad Banding of the pay structure
The plan is automatically void, because federal law prohibits per-order bonuses
explanation: Per-order bonuses lead to cherry-picking and rushed work, with no teamwork and no teaching. Lewis’s fix was a 4-tier maintenance pay system that rewarded seniors for bringing up the next tier.

prompt: Senior “wizard” technicians refuse to share their “little black book” of knowledge with newer workers. According to Sam Lewis, they do this because it protects their:
explanation: Knowledge = power = job security. The answer is to reward mentoring through tiered, skill-based pay.

prompt: Rivian entered Normal at $17/hr, quickly went to $22/hr, and forced local plants to raise their pay. This situation is an example of:
options: A labor-market shock driving external competitiveness
A rule requiring employers to match any new entrant’s wage within the same county
explanation: A new employer changed the local labor market, so other employers had to respond to stay competitive. Lewis told clients, “Your pay has to go up.”

prompt: According to Sam Lewis, a salary survey does NOT tell an organization:
options: Whether its rewards support the right behavior
Whether its pay is in the right range
explanation: Surveys answer only the competitiveness question. They also don’t tell you what different employees value.

prompt: A restaurant chain (e.g., Cracker Barrel) awards star pins to its servers. Which element of the total rewards portfolio is the chain using?
explanation: The total rewards portfolio is cash, benefits, flexibility, growth opportunities and recognition; star pins are Recognition. The goal is to send employees a coherent signal.

prompt: Sam Lewis used the DISC analogy to make which point about compensation design?
options: Organizations should hire only dominant personality types
Compensation should be designed for the whole team, not one type of person
Personality test results must always be used to set individual pay
None of the answer choices are correct
explanation: A room full of one personality type doesn’t work (the Jordan vs. Riley example), so pay plans should fit the whole team.

prompt: Performance pay fails when employees can’t influence the result. Competency pay fails when ______.
options: the salary survey is out of date
explanation: This is the “common trap” line from the Lewis notes: paying for a skill the company never uses. As he put it, don’t pay a PhD rocket scientist to assemble widgets.
